title: When people treat us superficially part 2
scripture_text: ‘’At that point some of the people of Jerusalem began to ask, “Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill? Here he is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying a word to him. Have the authorities really concluded that he is the Messiah? But we know where this man is from; when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.” Then Jesus, still teaching in the temple courts, cried out, “Yes, you know me, and you know where I am from. I am not here on my own authority, but he who sent me is true. You do not know him, but I know him because I am from him and he sent me.”
devotional:
The context of the passage

Jesus is at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem where the religious authorities have desires to kill him. There is a lot of tension and fear around the city. People are whispering and spreading rumours about Jesus. Halfway through the feast, Jesus goes to the temple area in order to address the hostility of the religious authorities. As he is speaking, he is interrupted by the people of Jerusalem who have questions about his identity.

Jesus' identity was one of the most controversial issues of the day. As Jesus defines his identity here, we should not be surprised at the growing hostility of the Jewish authorities. Their knowledge of Jesus was superficial, they said ‘’Have the authorities really concluded that he is the Messiah? But we know where this man is from; when the Messiah comes, no one will know where he is from.”

Their knowledge of Jesus was not based on any real, personal experience, but on hearsay and gossip.

The roots of superficiality

Often, superficiality stems from feelings of fear. When people feel threatened, or are not prepared to face their own problems, they can begin to question and belittle the identity of others. The people of Jerusalem were unable to accept what Jesus had been saying so they became hostile by being superficial about his identity. Their superficiality and hostility towards Jesus was rooted in the fact that they didn’t really know him:

They talked about him, not to him. ‘Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill?’ John 7:25. These remarks are neither a confession about Jesus' identity nor a testimony on his behalf. Rather they voice a question to each other.

Furthermore they stopped listening to what Jesus was saying. Remember, Jesus was still teaching at this point, and as he was speaking, they began to talk to each other. Their actions indicated that they didn’t think Jesus was worth listening to. They didn’t like what they were hearing so they switched off (like we often do), and turned their attention elsewhere.

John says 7:26 ‘At that point some of the people in Jerusalem began to ask..’

What ‘point’ is John referring to?

In the previous verse, Jesus says ‘Stop judging by mere appearance, and make right judgements.’ That’s the point at which they stop listening. Jesus was confronting their whole value system and mindset.

The people of Jerusalem were greatly influenced by the Pharisees who always judged or evaluated a person by their external appearance and behaviour. It seems as though they didn’t like the implications of what Jesus was saying. So, as a sign of their disapproval they stopped listening, refusing to give Jesus their full attention, They began to discuss him, knowing that he was able to hear what they were saying. This is a classic example of superficiality, and disdain for a person. This was an expression of rude disregard, that belittled Jesus and his teaching.

They refused to take any responsibility in wanting Jesus dead. We read that they were asking ‘Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill?’ The people of Jerusalem were not prepared to help Jesus, or stand up for him, even though they were aware of the plot against him. They were complicit in these murderous threats. Their lack of concern for Jesus made them as guilty as the religious leaders.

The negation of our responsibilities towards others will encourage superficiality. In superficial living there is always a ‘they,’ or a ‘him’ or a ‘he,’ or a ‘she,’ to blame, someone else is always responsible. There’s always someone else to ‘carry the can’, but it’s never us. Our superficiality prevents us from taking a good honest look at our own hearts, so we will automatically look for someone else to pin the blame on. Remember this was this same Jerusalem crowd that would eventually demand the blood and death of Jesus.

They allowed others to influence their opinions about Jesus, refusing to come to their own conclusions. As the people discussed the rumoured plans to kill Jesus, they wonder whether the leaders had changed their mind, for John tells us that Jesus is ‘speaking publicly and they are not saying a word to him’ John 7:26a. So the people ask ‘Have the authorities really concluded that he is the Christ?’ John 7:26b.

It appears that these people are not prepared to decide for themselves who Jesus was, but they prefer to be influenced by what their leaders might have been thinking.

There is a warning here for all who call themselves disciples of Jesus. We live in a time where Christians are not encouraged to think critically about their faith or consider why they believe what they believe. It’s too easy for us to sit in church, expecting to be spoon-fed, and then simply regurgitate what we’ve been told. We settle for second-hand faith, rather than first-hand experience of Jesus, which is always fatal. After all, faith without relationship is little more than dry orthodoxy. It hardens the soul and kills the spirit within.

We need to begin to think for ourselves and come to our own conclusions about Jesus and his truth. This does not mean that every person should arrive at their own private understanding of ‘the truth’. Biblical truth is best understood in the context of a seeking community who are eager to learn and share together. However, this is not a licence for passive passengers who refuse to engage their own hearts and minds in the quest to know the real Jesus.
prayer: Father help me to engage my mind in spiritual thinking.
